wines.name: Pinot Noir
wines.answer: Pinot Noir goes best with Gruyère, Comté, aged Gouda and prosciutto. Its light tannin and bright acid lift nutty, mild cheeses and silky cured meats without flattening them.
wines.intro: The most cheese-friendly red there is. Light body and soft tannin mean it won't bully delicate flavors, and its earthy, red-cherry fruit loves anything nutty or mushroomy.

wines.swap: Can't find one you like under $20? Try Beaujolais-Villages or an Oregon or Chilean Pinot. Same light body, often cheaper.

faq.a: Gruyère, Comté and aged Gouda: nutty, firm cheeses with some sweetness. Brie and other bloomy rinds work too if they're at room temperature.

faq.q: Does Pinot Noir go with charcuterie?
faq.a: Yes. Its soft tannin suits prosciutto, duck prosciutto and pâté. Skip very spicy salami, which makes it taste hot.

faq.q: Should Pinot Noir be chilled?
faq.a: Slightly. 55–60°F, about 20 minutes in the fridge, keeps the fruit fresh and the alcohol in check.

faq.q: Why do Stilton and port go together?
faq.a: Salt and sweetness balance each other: the cheese makes the wine taste less sweet and the wine softens the cheese's sharpness.

faq.q: Ruby or tawny port with cheese?
faq.a: Ruby for blue cheese and chocolate. Tawny's caramel and nut notes suit aged Gouda and walnuts.

faq.q: When should you serve port?
faq.a: At the end, with the blue cheese and dessert items. Small pours, 2–3 oz.

faq.q: What cheese goes with tawny port?
faq.a: Hard, aged cheeses with their own caramel and nut notes: aged Gouda, Comté, Gruyère and Parmigiano-Reggiano. Add walnuts or dried figs.

faq.q: Is port wine cheese the same as cheese with port?
faq.a: No. Port wine cheese is a red, spreadable cheddar-style cheese flavored with port. Cheese with port means serving a glass of port alongside cheese such as Stilton.

faq.q: How much port do you need for a cheese board?
faq.a: One 750 ml bottle gives about twelve 2 oz pours, enough for six people to have two small glasses each.

faq.q: Does port go with brie?
faq.a: Tawny port does: its caramel and nut notes suit rich triple-crème and ripe brie. Young ruby port is too sweet and fruity for mild brie; save it for blue cheese.

faq.q: What is a good inexpensive port for cheese?
faq.a: Kirkland 10 Year Tawny (about $17 at Costco) for aged Gouda and nuts, or Graham's Six Grapes Reserve ruby (about $27) for Stilton. See our best port wine guide for more.

sections.h: Why Stilton and port is the classic
sections.p: The pairing comes from Britain, where port has been the after-dinner wine for centuries and Stilton the after-dinner cheese. It works because opposites balance: the cheese is salty, sharp and creamy, the wine is sweet, rich and strong, and each one tames the other. The same logic makes port work with any salty blue, and with hard aged cheeses that have their own caramel notes.

sections.h: Port wine cheese is something else
sections.p: "Port wine cheese" or "red port cheese" is a spreadable, cheddar-style cheese colored red and flavored with port, sold in tubs and cheese balls. It is a party spread, not a pairing. Serve it on crackers with a glass of ruby port or a fruity red. Our picks: [the best port wine cheese spreads](/blog/best-port-wine-cheese/).

beers.answer: Dry hard cider pairs best with aged cheddar, Camembert, brie, Gruyère, pork pâté and ham. Apple acidity cuts rich cheese and pork the way a slice of apple does.
beers.intro: Gluten-free, crisp and fruity. Cider does what a fresh apple does on a board, which makes it one of the most cheese-friendly drinks there is.

cocktails.name: Cocktails & Spirits
cocktails.answer: The best cocktails for a charcuterie board are a dry martini, Aperol spritz, Negroni, old fashioned and gin and tonic. Bitter and citrusy drinks cut fat; brown spirits match aged cheese and smoky meat.
cocktails.intro: Cocktails are stronger than wine, so pair by flavor and keep pours small. Bitter aperitifs and citrusy drinks are the easiest; save brown spirits for the aged cheese and chocolate.

items.name: Dry martini
items.why: Cold, dry and briny. Olives are the garnish for a reason; salty almonds and Parmigiano stay in the same lane.

items.name: Aperol spritz
items.why: Bitter orange and bubbles: Italy's aperitivo drink with Italy's aperitivo board.

items.name: Negroni
items.why: Bitter, sweet and strong, it needs salty, savory Italian bites.

items.name: Old fashioned (bourbon or rye)
items.why: Caramel, vanilla and oak meet sharp cheese, smoke and sweet nuts.

items.name: Gin and tonic
items.why: Botanical and bitter-bright; it treats briny and fresh foods like a crisp white would.

items.name: Margarita / tequila
items.why: Lime and agave cut spicy, salty Mexican flavors.

items.name: Scotch (neat or with a splash)
items.why: Smoke and malt with Britain's big cheeses. Smoky Islay whisky loves smoked salmon.

items.name: Sherry (fino or amontillado)
items.why: Dry, nutty and salty: the tapas-bar drink with tapas-bar food.

faq.q: What cocktail goes with a charcuterie board?
faq.a: An Aperol spritz or dry martini for most boards; an old fashioned for aged cheese and smoked meat.

faq.q: What liquor goes with cheese?
faq.a: Bourbon and Scotch with aged cheddar and blue; dry sherry with Manchego; gin with fresh goat cheese.

faq.q: How strong should board cocktails be?
faq.a: Lighter than usual. Spritzes and highballs keep the palate fresh across a long board.

zero.name: Zero-Proof Pairings
zero.answer: The best non-alcoholic drinks for a charcuterie board are sparkling apple cider, black or green iced tea, kombucha, tart cherry spritz and sparkling water with citrus. Bubbles, acid and tannin do what wine does.
zero.intro: Wine works with cheese because of acid, bubbles and tannin. Plenty of alcohol-free drinks have the same three things, so the same pairing rules apply.

items.name: Sparkling apple cider (non-alcoholic)
items.why: Acid and bubbles, like Champagne or cider, with apple fruit that loves cheddar.

items.name: Black iced tea, unsweetened
items.why: Tea has tannin, just like red wine, so it softens with fat and aged cheese.

items.name: Green tea or jasmine tea
items.why: Light, grassy and gently bitter, like a Sauvignon Blanc.

items.name: Kombucha (ginger or plain)
items.why: Tangy and fizzy; it handles funk, smoke and pickles the way Riesling does.

items.name: Tart cherry or pomegranate spritz
items.why: Sweet-tart fruit balances salty blue cheese, like port.

items.name: Sparkling water with lemon or lime
items.why: Pure bubbles and acid reset your palate between salty bites.

items.name: Cold brew coffee
items.why: Roasty and bitter like a stout, for dessert boards.

faq.q: What non-alcoholic drink goes with charcuterie?
faq.a: Sparkling apple cider for most boards; unsweetened black iced tea for salami and aged cheese.

faq.q: Why does iced tea go with cheese?
faq.a: Black tea has tannin, the same drying compound in red wine, so it pairs the same way: fat and protein soften it.

faq.q: What's a good mocktail for a cheese board?
faq.a: A tart cherry or pomegranate spritz with blue cheese, or sparkling cider with cheddar and brie.

Why: big bubbles and minerals stand up to salt and fat

qa.q: What non-alcoholic drinks go with cheese?
a: Brie and soft cheese: sparkling apple cider

qa.q: Does ginger ale go with a charcuterie board?
a: Yes, if it is a dry or spicy ginger ale

Harder: very sweet sodas like cola or lemon-lime; sugar dulls the cheese
Fix: cut sweet sodas half and half with sparkling water

spirits.name: Whisky
spirits.seo_title: Whisky Pairing Chart: 13 Cheeses, Meats and Sweets
spirits.seo_description: A whisky pairing chart: 13 cheeses, meats and sweets that stand up to a 40% spirit, from aged cheddar and Stilton to dark chocolate, plus the 3 to skip.
spirits.serve: Neat or with a few drops of water, in a small pour. Room temperature, never over ice for a pairing.
spirits.answer: Whisky goes best with aged cheddar, aged gouda, stilton, dark chocolate and candied pecans. Whisky is far stronger than wine, so pair it with cheese that has age, salt and crystal crunch — anything soft or delicate disappears underneath it.
spirits.intro: Whisky is the hardest drink on a board to get right, because it arrives at roughly three times the strength of wine and most cheese simply surrenders to it. The cheeses that survive have two things in common: age and salt. A two-year cheddar, an aged gouda or a hard alpine wheel all have concentrated flavour and tyrosine crystals that give the palate something to push back with, and the long finish on a good malt then has somewhere to go. Pour small — an ounce is plenty — and give people water alongside, because palate fatigue arrives much faster than it does with wine. If the whisky is peated, treat the smoke as an ingredient in its own right and pair it like you would a smoked meat.

matches.why: A two-year cheddar has the salt, the acid and the crystal crunch to meet whisky head-on. The single safest pairing on this list.

A faintly bitter, tannic nut. It gives the palate something dry to land on between sips.

avoid.why: Milky and delicate. Whisky flattens it completely and you taste nothing but alcohol.
The bright acid in young goat cheese turns metallic against a high-proof spirit.

spirits.swap: No whisky in the house? An aged rum or a cognac pairs almost identically. For something lower in alcohol, a tawny port covers the same sweet-and-nutty ground.

faq.q: What cheese goes best with whisky?
faq.a: Aged cheddar, then aged gouda. Both have the salt, age and crystal texture to stand up to a spirit at 40% and over. Blue cheese is the other reliable answer, especially with a sweeter malt.

faq.q: Does whisky go with cheese at all?
faq.a: Yes, but it is less forgiving than wine. Stick to hard, aged cheese, keep the pours to about an ounce, and skip anything soft, fresh or milky — those get obliterated.

faq.q: Scotch or bourbon for a cheese board?
faq.a: Bourbon is easier. Its vanilla and caramel from new oak land naturally with aged gouda and candied nuts. Scotch is better if you want a smoky pairing, but a heavily peated Islay malt will dominate most of the board.

faq.q: Should I add water or ice to whisky for a pairing?
faq.a: A few drops of water, yes — it opens the aroma. Ice, no. The cold mutes both the whisky and the cheese, which is the opposite of what a pairing needs.

faq.q: How much whisky per person for a tasting?
faq.a: About half an ounce per pairing, and no more than four pairings. That is two ounces a head in total, which is one standard drink.

spirits.seo_description: Bourbon goes best with aged cheddar, aged Gouda, Maytag blue, country ham, candied pecans and dark chocolate. 12 matches, what to skip, and how to pour.
spirits.h1: Bourbon and cheese pairing: 12 matches and the 3 to skip
spirits.serve: Neat or with a few drops of water; ½–1 oz pours
spirits.answer: Bourbon goes best with aged cheddar, aged Gouda, a creamy American blue, country ham, candied pecans and dark chocolate. Its caramel and vanilla want aged, salty cheese with crunch.
spirits.intro: Bourbon must be made in the United States from at least 51% corn and aged in new charred oak, which gives it caramel, vanilla and baking-spice flavors. Those sweet notes make it the friendliest whiskey for cheese. Pair it like a dessert wine: aged, salty, nutty cheese and something toasted. Pour small, about an ounce, and put water out too.

spirits.swap: No bourbon? A rye whiskey is spicier and drier; pair it with Gruyère and aged Gouda. For lower alcohol, a tawny port covers the same caramel-and-nut ground.

faq.q: What cheese goes best with bourbon?
faq.a: Aged cheddar and aged Gouda: their nutty, caramel flavors match the barrel. A creamy American blue like Maytag is the bold choice.

faq.q: Can you put bourbon on a charcuterie board?
faq.a: Yes. Serve ½–1 oz pours with water on the side, and build the board around aged cheese, country ham, pecans and dark chocolate.

faq.q: What makes bourbon different from other whiskey?
faq.a: It must be made in the US from at least 51% corn and aged in new charred oak containers. That's where the sweetness and vanilla come from.

faq.q: What's the difference between bourbon and Scotch with cheese?
faq.a: Bourbon is sweeter, so it suits salty, aged cheese. Smoky Scotch suits blue and smoked cheese. More: [whiskey and cheese pairing](/blog/whiskey-and-cheese-pairing/).
